entries.answer_gold: Yes. Phylactery Lich and Solemnity enter the battlefield at the same time. Solemnity's effect must exist before Phylactery Lich enters the battlefield in order to prevent Bronze Sable from getting a counter.

entries.question: Ashley controls [Tatterkite]. Ashley casts [Genesis Wave], putting [Phylactery Lich] and [Humility] onto the battlefield. Can they put a phylactery counter on Tatterkite?
entries.reason: Both conclude no phylactery counter is placed because Humility and Phylactery Lich enter simultaneously and Humility removes the Lich's "as this creature enters" ability so there is no effect to put a counter.
entries.answer:
Short answer: No phylactery counter gets put anywhere at all — because Humility enters at the same time as Phylactery Lich and strips Phylactery Lich of its "As this creature enters, put a phylactery counter on an artifact you control" ability, so there is no counter-placing effect to apply. (Ironically, Humility also strips Tatterkite of "This creature can't have counters put on it," so Tatterkite would have been a legal choice if the ability still existed.)

Why:

1. All the permanents from Genesis Wave enter the battlefield simultaneously [Genesis Wave ruling #5]. So Humility is already on the battlefield as Phylactery Lich arrives.

2. Humility's "All creatures lose all abilities and have base power and toughness 1/1" is a continuous effect applied in layer 6, the ability-removing layer [613.1f], and it removes every creature ability, including mana abilities [Humility ruling #1]. Phylactery Lich is a creature, so as it enters it has no abilities — neither the "as this creature enters" counter ability nor the "when you control no permanents with phylactery counters" state trigger. That state trigger being gone also means Phylactery Lich won't be sacrificed for lacking a phylactery counter (contrast [Phylactery Lich ruling #0], which assumes the ability is intact).

3. Tatterkite: its ability normally stops any kind of counter, not just -1/-1 counters [Tatterkite ruling #1], and it functions as the object enters as well as on the battlefield [113.6i]; an effect that would put a counter on it simply doesn't affect it [Tatterkite ruling #2]. But Tatterkite is a creature, so Humility removes that ability too in layer 6 [613.1f]. Note that Humility grants nothing and removes rather than prevents, so this is ability removal, not a "can't" effect fight [101.2a].

Timing/ordering note: I'm assuming Humility and Phylactery Lich truly enter together off the same Genesis Wave resolution, which is what Genesis Wave does. If instead Humility were already on the battlefield first, the result is identical. If Phylactery Lich somehow entered while Humility was not yet on the battlefield, its as-enters ability would work and you could put the phylactery counter on Tatterkite only if Tatterkite's ability were already removed; otherwise Tatterkite would be an illegal home for the counter and no counter would be placed [Tatterkite ruling #2]. Also, Tatterkite is fine as a choice on the "already on the battlefield" requirement — you may not choose an artifact entering simultaneously with Phylactery Lich [Phylactery Lich ruling #1], and Tatterkite was already there.

This analysis is the same whether the game has two players or more; nothing here depends on opponents' choices.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Phylactery Lich and Humility enter the battlefield at the same time. Tatterkite had the ability that prevents it from getting counters immediately before Phylactery Lich entered the battlefield, which is when it matters.

entries.question: Avery controls [The One Ring] and casts [Teferi's Protection] then casts a second The One Ring. What happens at the start of the next turn?
entries.reason: The candidate says only the Ring(s) remaining on the battlefield will trigger in the upkeep, whereas the correct ruling is that both triggers go on the stack when they trigger and the trigger for the Ring that is later sacrificed still resolves using last-known information.
entries.answer:
Direct answer: At the start of Avery's next turn, the Teferi's Protection effects end (Avery's life total can change again and the protection from everything from Teferi's Protection expires), and then, before Avery untaps during the untap step, the first The One Ring and every other permanent that phased out phases in — still indestructible and still with whatever burden counters it had. Because both copies of The One Ring are then on the battlefield under Avery's control at the same time, Avery must keep one and put the other into the graveyard; indestructible does not help against that, since it isn't destruction. Then, in the upkeep step, each The One Ring still on the battlefield triggers its "lose 1 life for each burden counter" ability.

Details and assumptions:
- Phasing means the permanent is treated as though it doesn't exist: it can't be targeted, its static abilities do nothing, its triggered abilities can't trigger, and it can't attack or block [Teferi's Protection ruling #5]. That's why the phased-out first The One Ring did not stop Avery from having the second The One Ring on the battlefield in the meantime, and why the phased-out copy's upkeep trigger did nothing while phased out.
- Phased-out permanents phase in as Avery's next untap step begins, with counters intact and with any Auras/Equipment that phased out with them [Teferi's Protection ruling #14][Teferi's Protection ruling #15]. Phasing in causes no "enters the battlefield" triggers, so the phased-in The One Ring does not re-trigger its "When The One Ring enters" protection ability [Teferi's Protection ruling #20].
- The second The One Ring, cast after Teferi's Protection, did give Avery protection from everything on entry, but a second instance of protection from the same quality is redundant [702.16m], so it expires along with everything else in the sense that Avery simply has protection from everything until Avery's next turn, then loses it. If Avery's untap step is somehow skipped, the protection and life-total lock still end as the turn begins, but the phased-out permanents wait for the next actual untap step [Teferi's Protection ruling #21].
- Caveat on grounding: the "legend rule" state-based action itself was not included in the rules provided to me (the context includes only the analogous world rule and Role rules, [704.5k] and [704.5y]/[303.7a]), so treat the "keep one, bin the other" step as the standard legend-rule outcome rather than something I can cite here.
- Timing note: I read "the start of the next turn" as Avery's next turn, which is what Teferi's Protection's "until your next turn" duration keys off. If instead the next turn is an opponent's turn, nothing changes yet — Avery's permanents stay phased out and Avery keeps protection from everything and an unchangeable life total through that turn.
- Player count: nothing here depends on the number of opponents; the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The One Ring will phase back in during the untap step. Then all triggered abilities will go onto the stack, then before Avery gets priority they will have to sacrifice a The One Ring to state-based actions. When the triggers resolve the trigger affiliated with the sacrificed The One Ring will use last known information to determine how many counters were on it, and how much life Avery should lose.

entries.question: Amaya controls [Dralnu, Lich Lord], [Furnace of Rath] and six [Snow-Covered Forest]s. Nico casts [Incinerate] targeting Dralnu, Lich Lord. If Amaya chooses to sacrifice Furnace of Rath, how many other permanents will they need to sacrifice?
entries.reason: Both answers say Amaya chooses the order of replacement effects, resulting in either sacrificing two other permanents (Dralnu first) or five other permanents (Furnace first).
entries.answer:
Five other permanents — six sacrifices total, one of which is Furnace of Rath.

Why: Incinerate would deal 3 damage to Dralnu, Lich Lord. Both Furnace of Rath and Dralnu, Lich Lord's own ability are replacement effects that modify how that damage would be dealt, so Amaya (the affected permanent's controller) chooses the order they apply [Furnace of Rath ruling #4]. I'm assuming the order the question implies: Furnace of Rath applies first, doubling 3 to 6 damage (the damage still counts as coming from Incinerate, not Furnace of Rath [Furnace of Rath ruling #1]). Then Dralnu, Lich Lord's replacement effect converts that into "sacrifice that many permanents" — 6 permanents.

Amaya controls 8 permanents (Dralnu, Lich Lord, Furnace of Rath, and six Snow-Covered Forests), so 6 is payable. Sacrificing means moving a permanent you control from the battlefield straight to its owner's graveyard; it isn't destruction, so regeneration-type effects don't apply [701.21a]. If Furnace of Rath is one of the six, Amaya sacrifices 5 more permanents — and Dralnu, Lich Lord itself is allowed to be one of them [Dralnu, Lich Lord ruling #4].

If instead Amaya applied Dralnu, Lich Lord's effect first, there would be no damage left for Furnace of Rath to double, and only 3 permanents would be sacrificed (2 others besides Furnace of Rath). Note also that if the required number ever exceeded Amaya's permanent count, they'd simply sacrifice all permanents they control [Dralnu, Lich Lord ruling #13]. Nothing here depends on the number of players.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Two or five, Amaya's choice.

Both Dralnu, Lich Lord and Furnace of Rath have replacement effects that modify how the game handles damage that is being dealt to Dralnu, Lich Lord. As Amaya is the controller of the affected object, Amaya will choose which order to apply the replacement effects in. If Amaya chooses to apply Dralnu, Lich Lord's effect first, the 3 damage will be converted into sacrificing three permanents, and Furnace of Rath will no longer apply to that event since there's no longer any damage being dealt. If they chooses to apply Furnace of Rath first, then the three damage will be doubled to six damage, and then will be replaced by sacrificing six permanents.

Whether Amaya chooses to sacrifice Furnace of Rath or not is irrelevant, as all replacement effects are applied to the event before anything is actually sacrificed.

entries.question: Aubrey and Arely are playing 2HG. Aubrey attacks with [Coral Commando] and Arely casts [Flash Conscription] to gain control of Coral Commando after it's been declared as an attacker in the declare attackers step. Is it still attacking?
entries.reason: Both correctly conclude that when Arely gains control of Coral Commando it changes controller and is removed from combat, so it stops being an attacking creature.
entries.answer:
No — Coral Commando stops attacking. When Arely casts Flash Conscription and gains control of Coral Commando, that change of controller removes Coral Commando from combat: a permanent is removed from combat if its controller changes, and a creature removed from combat stops being an attacking, blocking, blocked, and/or unblocked creature [506.4a]. So Coral Commando deals no combat damage in the combat damage step and won't be dealt damage by blockers.

Details and assumptions:
- I'm assuming the timing given: Coral Commando was legally declared as an attacker in the declare attackers step, and Flash Conscription resolved afterward (still during that combat, before combat damage). Under that timing Coral Commando is out of combat for the rest of the phase. If instead Flash Conscription had resolved before attackers were declared, Coral Commando simply would never have been declared by Aubrey at all (Arely would control it, and Arely could attack with it if Arely were the active player, thanks to the haste it gains).
- Note that although Arely now controls Coral Commando, nothing puts it back into combat. Rule 508.4 only makes a creature attacking if an effect says so or it's put onto the battlefield attacking; Flash Conscription does neither — it only untaps, gains control, and grants haste. Also, once a creature has been declared as an attacker, effects are what remove it from combat, not a re-declaration [506.4a].
- Aubrey has still "attacked" for the purposes of anything that triggered on the declaration, since Coral Commando was declared as an attacker attacking that opponent [508.6].
- Since this is Two-Headed Giant (shared team turns), the attacking team declares one combined set of attackers and announces what each attacker is attacking [805.10b]; that doesn't change the outcome here — the control change still removes Coral Commando from combat. The same answer applies in a plain two-player game.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. A creature that changes controllers is removed from combat. Even though Aubrey and Arely are on the same team and are both allowed to be attacking with creatures, they are different players and therefore Arely gaining control of Aubrey's creature still qualifies as a control change.

entries.question: Nicolas controls [Razorfield Thresher], [Lake of the Dead], and [Veinfire Borderpost]. Aubrey controls [Omniscience] and casts [Casualties of War], choosing Razorfield Thresher as the artifact target and the creature target. Then they cast [Radiate], targeting Casualties of War. What will be destroyed after all spells and abilities have resolved?
entries.reason: The candidate is wrong — Radiate will produce a copy that can target Veinfire Borderpost (as the artifact) and Razorfield Thresher (as the creature), so both permanents are destroyed.
entries.answer:
Only Razorfield Thresher is destroyed.

Why: Aubrey's Casualties of War has two chosen modes, "Destroy target artifact" and "Destroy target creature," and both instances of "target" point at the same permanent, Razorfield Thresher. That means it does target only a single permanent, so it's a legal target for Radiate.

Radiate then copies the spell "for each other permanent or player the spell could target," and each copy must target a different one of those permanents/players. Because Casualties of War as cast needs one object to be legal for *both* the artifact target and the creature target, the only permanents it "could target" are artifact creatures. Among Nicolas's permanents, Lake of the Dead is a land (not an artifact, not a creature) and Veinfire Borderpost is an artifact but not a creature, so neither could be a legal target for both instances of "target." Aubrey's Omniscience is an enchantment, also not targetable by the chosen modes. So there is no "other permanent or player the spell could target," and Radiate creates zero copies; Radiate itself does nothing further.

Casualties of War then resolves and destroys Razorfield Thresher (the same permanent for both modes; a permanent can only be destroyed once). Any abilities that trigger on it being destroyed or leaving the battlefield are put on the stack only after Casualties of War finishes resolving [Casualties of War ruling #1], and leaves-the-battlefield triggers "look back in time" at the game state just before it left [603.10a].

One note on how a copy would fare if such a permanent existed: a copy pointed at something that isn't legal for either target instance simply wouldn't resolve; if it were legal for one instance but not the other, it would still resolve and apply only the part it's legal for [608.2b].

Multiplayer: this answer covers Nicolas's and Aubrey's permanents. At a larger table, Radiate would make one copy for each *other* artifact creature on the battlefield that anyone controls (each copy targeting a different one with both modes), and each of those would be destroyed too. Note that Omniscience only affects paying the mana cost; it doesn't change targeting at all.

entries.question: Alonso controls [Spark Double] and casts [Clone]. Alonso would like to have Clone copy Spark Double, then they would like to apply the replacement effect Clone inherited from Spark Double and have it copy Spark Double again. If Alonso has Clone copy Spark Double a total of four times, how many +1/+1 counters will Clone enter the battlefield with?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Clone ends up with one +1/+1 counter because only the final copy application’s "except it enters with an additional +1/+1 counter" takes effect.
entries.answer:
Clone enters the battlefield with exactly one +1/+1 counter, no matter how many times Alonso re-applies the copy effect.

Why: Spark Double's text is "You may have this creature enter as a copy of a creature or planeswalker you control, except it enters with an additional +1/+1 counter on it if it's a creature..." That "except" clause is an additional effect, not a modification of copiable characteristics. Rule 707.9e says that if another copy effect is applied to the object after applying the copy effect carrying such an exception, the exception's effect doesn't happen.

So when Clone copies Spark Double the first time, Clone becomes a copy of Spark Double (Spark Double ruling #7 / Clone ruling #5 confirm chained copying works) and gains Spark Double's copy replacement effect. When Alonso uses that inherited effect to copy Spark Double again, that later copy effect wipes out the earlier exception — no counter from the first application. The same happens for the second and third applications. Only the fourth and final application of the copy effect has no subsequent copy effect applied after it, so only its exception happens: one additional +1/+1 counter (Spark Double ruling #3, which says a Spark Double copying a creature enters with a +1/+1 counter plus any counters from abilities it copied).

So the count doesn't scale with the number of iterations: 1 counter, plus any counters granted by "enters with" abilities of the thing finally copied (here Spark Double has none of its own, such as amplify per 702.38a). Clone also isn't legendary, and that exception *is* copiable (Spark Double ruling #6).

This answer doesn't depend on player count — it's purely about how Clone enters, and Spark Double's own restriction is that the copied permanent must be one Alonso controls, so opponents' permanents aren't eligible in any case.

entries.answer_gold: One. Spark Double has a copy effect that includes an exception (entering with a +1/+1 counter). If another copy effect is applied afterwards, the exception from the first effect will not happen.

entries.question: Nickolas controls a [Nyx Herald] enchanted by [Drake Umbra]. Ainsley casts [Fracturing Gust]. How much life do they gain?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Nyx Herald is saved by Drake Umbra’s replacement effect and only Drake Umbra is actually destroyed once by Fracturing Gust, so Ainsley gains 2 life.
entries.answer:
Ainsley gains 2 life from this pair of permanents — 2 life for Drake Umbra only, and nothing for Nyx Herald, which isn't destroyed.

Why: Fracturing Gust tries to destroy all artifacts and enchantments, which includes both Drake Umbra (an enchantment Aura) and Nyx Herald (an enchantment creature). Drake Umbra's umbra armor is a replacement effect: if the enchanted creature would be destroyed, instead remove all damage from it and destroy Drake Umbra. Because Fracturing Gust would destroy Nyx Herald and Drake Umbra at the same time, umbra armor saves Nyx Herald, and Fracturing Gust ends up destroying Drake Umbra in two different ways simultaneously — the result is the same as destroying it once [Drake Umbra ruling #4]. Umbra armor's effect is mandatory [Drake Umbra ruling #1].

Since Nyx Herald remains on the battlefield, Ainsley gains no life for it — Fracturing Gust only gives 2 life per permanent actually destroyed by it [Fracturing Gust ruling #0]. Drake Umbra counts once, not twice, so that's 2 life.

Of course, if any other artifacts or enchantments are on the battlefield, add 2 more life for each one Fracturing Gust actually destroys.

Multiplayer note: this outcome doesn't depend on player count; Fracturing Gust hits every player's artifacts and enchantments, so at a bigger table the total is 2 life per permanent destroyed anywhere. In a Two-Headed Giant game, the life gain happens to Ainsley individually but is applied to their team's shared life total [810.9].

entries.question: Avery controls [Corpsejack Menace] and casts [Rescuer Sphinx], choosing to return Corpsejack Menace to their hand. How many +1/+1 counters will Rescuer Sphinx enter the battlefield with?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Sphinx enters with one counter, which contradicts the correct ruling that Corpsejack Menace's replacement effect still applies and Rescuer Sphinx enters with two +1/+1 counters.
entries.answer:
Rescuer Sphinx enters with just one +1/+1 counter, not two.

Rescuer Sphinx's own text is a replacement effect that modifies how it enters: "As this creature enters, you may return a nonland permanent you control to its owner's hand. If you do, this creature enters with a +1/+1 counter on it." Avery chooses Corpsejack Menace as that permanent, and it goes to the owner's hand as part of applying that effect — this all happens while Rescuer Sphinx is entering, and no player may take actions between the choice and Rescuer Sphinx being on the battlefield with its counter [Rescuer Sphinx ruling #2]. An effect modifying how a permanent enters the battlefield can indeed cause other objects to change zones [614.13b].

Corpsejack Menace's doubling ability ("If one or more +1/+1 counters would be put on a creature you control, twice that many +1/+1 counters are put on it instead") is a static replacement effect that functions only while Corpsejack Menace is on the battlefield. Because Avery has already returned Corpsejack Menace to hand as part of Rescuer Sphinx entering, it is not on the battlefield to double the counter, so Rescuer Sphinx ends up with a single +1/+1 counter and is a 4/3 flyer.

For contrast: if Avery had returned some other nonland permanent and left Corpsejack Menace on the battlefield, Rescuer Sphinx would enter with two +1/+1 counters, since a creature that would enter with +1/+1 counters enters with twice that many [Corpsejack Menace ruling #0] (and four times with two Corpsejack Menaces [Corpsejack Menace ruling #1]).

Note also that Avery couldn't have chosen a permanent entering simultaneously with Rescuer Sphinx — only permanents already on the battlefield are legal choices [Rescuer Sphinx ruling #0]. Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

entries.answer_gold: Two. Both cards have a replacement effect. Avery will choose whether they are returning a permanent, but won't actually complete the action until Rescuer Sphinx enters the battlefield. Therefore Corpsejack Menace will still apply to the +1/+1 counter being from Rescuer Sphinx's ability.

entries.question: Arabella casts [Mind's Desire]. In response, Neil casts [Lim-Dûl's Vault]. How many copies of Mind's Desire are created when the storm trigger resolves?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude storm only counts spells cast before Mind's Desire, so Lim-Dûl's Vault cast in response doesn't increase the storm count and results in zero copies.
entries.answer:
Zero copies — assuming Mind's Desire was the first spell cast this turn. Storm counts only spells that were cast *before* the spell with storm this turn ([702.40a]), and Neil's Lim-Dûl's Vault was cast afterward (in response), so it is not counted at all.

Details:
- Storm is a triggered ability that functions on the stack: "When you cast this spell, copy it for each other spell that was cast before it this turn" ([702.40a]). The trigger goes on the stack above Mind's Desire; Neil casting Lim-Dûl's Vault in response doesn't change the pool of earlier spells.
- Any spells cast earlier in the turn by *any* player would count, including spells cast from zones other than hand and spells that were countered ([Mind's Desire ruling #3]). So if, say, two spells had already been cast before Arabella's Mind's Desire this turn, the storm trigger would make 2 copies. With none, it makes 0 and the trigger simply resolves doing nothing.
- The copies are put directly onto the stack and aren't cast, so they never count toward a later storm spell's tally ([Mind's Desire ruling #4], [707.10b]). Each copy can be countered individually, and countering the original Mind's Desire doesn't remove the copies ([Mind's Desire ruling #5]); countering the storm trigger itself does prevent all copies ([Mind's Desire ruling #2]).
- Timing note: I'm reading the sequence as Mind's Desire cast first, then Lim-Dûl's Vault cast in response. If instead Neil had cast Lim-Dûl's Vault first and Arabella then cast Mind's Desire, Lim-Dûl's Vault would be an earlier spell and storm would create 1 copy (plus one for any other earlier spell).
- Player count doesn't matter here: storm counts spells cast by all players, so the same reasoning applies in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table — just add any spells other opponents cast earlier in the turn.

entries.answer_gold: 0. The storm trigger only cares about spells cast before the spell that caused it to trigger.

entries.question: Aubrey casts [Bitter Ordeal], targeting Natasha. At their first opportunity, Aubrey sacrifices their [Westvale Abbey]. How many cards will Aubrey be able to exile from Natasha's library?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling that two cards are exiled (the original spell plus one copy) provided Westvale Abbey is in the graveyard before the gravestorm trigger resolves and correctly explains gravestorm's timing.
entries.answer:
Short answer: two cards — the original Bitter Ordeal exiles one card, and the single gravestorm copy exiles a second, assuming Aubrey's Westvale Abbey actually reaches the graveyard before the gravestorm trigger resolves and Natasha's library has at least two cards.

How that adds up:

- Gravestorm on Bitter Ordeal reads "When you cast this spell, copy it for each permanent put into a graveyard this turn." Aubrey's first opportunity to act is with that triggered ability still on the stack, so a sacrifice made then happens before the count is taken, giving one permanent (Westvale Abbey) in a graveyard this turn, hence one copy.
- Each of the two Bitter Ordeal objects instructs Aubrey to search Natasha's library for a card and exile it. Searching a hidden zone for a quantity of cards means finding that many cards, or as many as possible if the zone doesn't hold enough [701.23d], and an effect that can't be fully performed does as much as possible [609.3]. So if Natasha's library is down to one card, only one card gets exiled overall; an empty library means none.
- Important caveat about the sacrifice: Westvale Abbey's own ability "{5}, {T}, Sacrifice five creatures: Transform this land, then untap it" sacrifices five *creatures*, not the land itself, and transforming does not put Westvale Abbey into a graveyard. For Westvale Abbey to count for gravestorm, Aubrey needs some outside effect that sacrifices the land. If instead Aubrey activates that ability and sacrifices five creatures, five permanents were put into a graveyard this turn, giving five copies plus the original — six cards exiled from Natasha's library (again, as many as possible if her library is smaller).
- Timing alternative: if the sacrifice somehow happened only after the gravestorm trigger had already resolved, it wouldn't be counted at all and Bitter Ordeal would exile just one card.

Player count: nothing here changes between a two-player game and a multiplayer table, since Bitter Ordeal targets a single player (Natasha) and gravestorm counts permanents put into any graveyard this turn.

Note on grounding: the provided context has no numbered rule for gravestorm itself, so the copy-count timing above is my stated assumption rather than a cited rule; the search/exile portion is rules-grounded.

entries.answer_gold: 2. Gravestorm cares about the number of permanents put into the graveyard before the trigger resolves.

entries.question: Ainsley activates [Priest of Forgotten Gods]'s ability, but doesn't choose a target for the first part. Can Nickolas respond to the ability?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion that the ability still requires targets for mana-ability purposes and therefore goes on the stack (so Nickolas can respond) even if zero targets are chosen.
entries.answer:
Yes. Nickolas can respond. Even with zero targets chosen, Priest of Forgotten Gods's ability goes on the stack and can be responded to.

Why: Priest of Forgotten Gods's ability reads "Any number of target players each lose 2 life and sacrifice a creature of their choice. You add {B}{B} and draw a card." "Any number of target players" permits choosing zero targets; a spell or ability like this is still said to require targets, but is only actually "targeted" if one or more targets were chosen [115.6]. So Ainsley may legally activate it with no targets and will still add {B}{B} and draw a card [Priest of Forgotten Gods ruling #0].

Crucially, because the ability *could* have targets, it is not a mana ability, so it does not resolve immediately outside the stack the way an activated mana ability would [605.3b]. It uses the stack and can be responded to even when no targets were chosen [Priest of Forgotten Gods ruling #1]. That means after Ainsley activates it, Ainsley retains priority and then players in turn order get priority, and Nickolas may cast instants or activate abilities in response — including removal on Priest of Forgotten Gods, though that won't stop the already-activated ability from resolving.

This is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table; with more than two players, every opponent gets a chance to respond in turn order, not just Nickolas.

One note on targeting: if Ainsley had chosen targets, players who can't sacrifice a creature are still legal targets and still lose 2 life [Priest of Forgotten Gods ruling #2].

entries.answer_gold: Yes. One of the qualifications for being a mana ability is that the ability doesn't require a target. Priest of Forgotten Gods's ability is still considered to require targets even if zero targets were chosen for it.

entries.question: Analia controls [Volrath's Shapeshifter] and [Muldrotha, the Gravetide], and the top card of their graveyard is [Grid Monitor]. Can Analia cast the Grid Monitor?
entries.reason: Both conclude Analia cannot cast Grid Monitor — the candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling that a Volrath's Shapeshifter-imposed prohibition on casting creature spells prevents casting despite Muldrotha's permission.
entries.answer:
No. Analia can't cast Grid Monitor.

Why: because the top card of Analia's graveyard is Grid Monitor, a creature card, Volrath's Shapeshifter has the full text of Grid Monitor (plus "{2}: Discard a card") [Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #1, Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #5]. That text includes "You can't cast creature spells," and Volrath's Shapeshifter is on the battlefield, so that static restriction applies to Analia.

Grid Monitor is an Artifact Creature card, and "creature spell" means any spell with the card type Creature, even if it also has another type such as Artifact [Grid Monitor ruling #1]. So a Grid Monitor spell is a creature spell no matter what.

Muldrotha, the Gravetide would otherwise give permission to cast it from the graveyard as either Analia's artifact-spell or creature-spell play for the turn [Muldrotha, the Gravetide ruling #0, Muldrotha, the Gravetide ruling #7], but choosing to "count it as" the artifact permission doesn't change the spell's types — it is still a creature spell. A player can begin to cast a spell only if a rule or effect allows it and no rule or effect prohibits it [601.3]; Volrath's Shapeshifter (as Grid Monitor) prohibits it, so the prohibition wins over Muldrotha, the Gravetide's permission.

Side note on timing: this holds as long as Grid Monitor is the top card of the graveyard at the moment Analia would begin casting. If Analia first changed the top graveyard card (e.g., by discarding with the "{2}: Discard a card" ability so a noncreature card is on top), Volrath's Shapeshifter reverts to a 0/1 with no restriction [Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #0] — but then Grid Monitor is no longer the top card, so Muldrotha, the Gravetide's permission isn't limited to the top card anyway and Analia could cast Grid Monitor from anywhere in the graveyard, since Muldrotha, the Gravetide doesn't require it to be on top.

This analysis doesn't depend on player count — it's the same in a two-player or multiplayer game, since only Analia's own permanents are involved.

entries.answer_gold: No. Analia must be legally allowed to cast a spell in order to begin casting it. None of the exceptions in [601.3] apply here.

entries.question: Antoine owns an [Eternal Scourge] that was exiled by Nico's [Ixalan's Binding]. Can Antoine cast it?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Antoine cannot cast the exiled Eternal Scourge because Ixalan's Binding's prohibition on opponents casting spells with that name prevents beginning to cast it despite the card's permission.
entries.answer:
No. Antoine cannot cast that Eternal Scourge (or any other card named Eternal Scourge) while it remains exiled by Nico's Ixalan's Binding.

Why: Eternal Scourge says "You may cast this card from exile," which is a permission, and you still must follow normal timing and pay its {3} cost [Eternal Scourge ruling #2]. But Ixalan's Binding says "Your opponents can't cast spells with the same name as the exiled card." A player can begin to cast a spell only if a rule or effect allows it AND no rule or effect prohibits it [601.3]. Since Antoine is an opponent of Nico (Ixalan's Binding's controller), the prohibition applies and overrides the permission granted by Eternal Scourge's own text.

Notes:
- This holds in both two-player and multiplayer games: the lock applies to each opponent of Ixalan's Binding's controller. Nico (and, in multiplayer, Nico's teammates/other non-opponents) would not be stopped by the Binding's restriction, though Eternal Scourge's "you may cast this card from exile" only grants permission to its owner/the exiled card's controller-permission holder, so in practice nobody else gets to cast it either.
- If Ixalan's Binding leaves the battlefield, the exiled Eternal Scourge returns to the battlefield immediately [Ixalan's Binding ruling #4], so it doesn't linger in exile for Antoine to cast.
- The name-matching is based on the card's name as it exists in exile [Ixalan's Binding ruling #2], so any other Eternal Scourge Antoine draws is also uncastable while the Binding is out.

entries.answer_gold: No. Antoine must be legally allowed to cast a spell in order to begin casting it. The exceptions in [601.3] do not apply here.

entries.question: Avery manifests the top card of their library with [Soul Summons]. Then, they mutate [Trumpeting Gnarr] targeting the manifested creature. What are the characteristics of the resulting creature if Avery chooses to put the manifested creature on top?
entries.reason: The candidate incorrectly says the merged permanent gains Trumpeting Gnarr’s abilities and that its mutate trigger fires, while the correct ruling is it’s a face-down 2/2 colorless creature with no abilities and Trumpeting Gnarr’s triggered ability does not trigger.
entries.answer:
The resulting permanent is a single mutated creature that looks like the face-down manifested card: a 2/2 colorless creature with no name, no creature types, no mana cost, and mana value 0 — but it has the abilities of both components, i.e. Trumpeting Gnarr's mutate ability and "Whenever this creature mutates, create a 3/3 green Beast creature token."

Why: when the mutating Trumpeting Gnarr spell resolves with a legal target, it doesn't enter the battlefield; it merges with the manifested creature to form one object represented by both cards, and Avery chooses the order [702.140c, 608.3d, 730.2a]. Because Avery puts the manifested (face-down) card on top, all characteristics other than abilities are derived from that topmost component [702.140e, 730.2a], and a face-down manifested permanent is a 2/2 colorless creature with no name, mana cost, creature types, or abilities, mana value 0 [Soul Summons ruling #8]. Abilities are the exception: a mutated permanent has all abilities of each card representing it [702.140e], so the Trumpeting Gnarr card underneath still contributes its two abilities even though it isn't the top card.

That mutate trigger does go off: an ability that triggers whenever a creature mutates triggers when a spell merges with a creature as a result of a resolving mutating creature spell, so Avery creates one 3/3 green Beast token [702.140d].

Also note Avery can still turn the manifested top card face up as a special action any time they have priority, by revealing it's a creature card and paying its mana cost [Soul Summons ruling #6, Soul Summons ruling #2]; if they do, the topmost component's face-up characteristics (name, colors, types, power/toughness) become the mutated permanent's characteristics, and it keeps Trumpeting Gnarr's abilities on top of its own. If the manifested card isn't a creature card, it can't be turned face up [Soul Summons ruling #1].

This answer doesn't depend on the number of players; mutate targets a non-Human creature with the same owner as the spell, so it works the same at a two-player or multiplayer table [702.140a].

entries.answer_gold: It is a 2/2 colorless face-down creature with no abilities. It is face-down because the topmost object is face-down, and this status defines its characteristics. This notably means that Trumpeting Gnarr's triggered ability won't trigger.

entries.question: Nayeli controls a [Yixlid Jailer]. Ariel has a [Golgari Brownscale] in their graveyard and returns it to their hand with [Disturbing Plot]. Does Ariel gain 2 life?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Ariel doesn't gain 2 life because Yixlid Jailer removes Brownscale's abilities in the graveyard so its "put into your hand from your graveyard" triggered ability can't exist.
entries.answer:
No — Ariel gains no life. Yixlid Jailer says "Cards in graveyards lose all abilities," so while Golgari Brownscale sits in Ariel's graveyard it has no abilities at all, including its "When this card is put into your hand from your graveyard, you gain 2 life" triggered ability.

That ability is one that must trigger while the card is still in the graveyard (the trigger event is leaving the graveyard for the hand), so the game looks at Golgari Brownscale in the graveyard to see whether it has the ability — and thanks to Yixlid Jailer, it doesn't. This matches the principle in [Yixlid Jailer ruling #4]: abilities that trigger on the object moving out of / into the graveyard from somewhere other than the battlefield are looked for in the graveyard, and Yixlid Jailer stops them from triggering at all. Contrast [Yixlid Jailer ruling #6]: only abilities that trigger from the battlefield escape Yixlid Jailer, which isn't the case here.

Disturbing Plot returning Golgari Brownscale is just an ordinary return-to-hand, so nothing else grants the ability, and no life gain event occurs at all — not even 0 life (see [119.3], [119.9]). It doesn't matter that Nayeli, not Ariel, controls Yixlid Jailer; its static effect applies to cards in all graveyards.

If Ariel later casts Golgari Brownscale or it otherwise reaches the battlefield, it has its abilities again there — but that gives no retroactive life gain. Note also that if Disturbing Plot is conspired and copied, targeting Golgari Brownscale again does nothing since it's already in hand.

This answer is the same at any table size; nothing here depends on the number of players.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Golgari Brownscale's trigger cares about the game state immediately before it triggered. At that time it was in the graveyard, and the trigger didn't exist.

entries.question: Aryana has taken control of an [Ahn-Crop Crasher] from Noe with [Tibalt, the Fiend-Blooded], which Aryana exerts. After Aryana ends their turn, will it untap during Noe's untap step?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same ruling as the reference: exert prevents untapping only during the exerting player's next untap step, so once control returns to Noe Ahn-Crop Crasher will untap on Noe's untap step.
entries.answer:
Yes. Ahn-Crop Crasher will untap normally during Noe's untap step. Exert means "you choose to have it not untap during your next untap step" — the untap step of the player who exerted it, i.e. Aryana [701.43a]. Because Tibalt, the Fiend-Blooded's third ability only gains control of Ahn-Crop Crasher until end of turn, control reverts to Noe when Aryana's turn ends, and Ahn-Crop Crasher is never around under Aryana's control for Aryana's own next untap step. Exert's effect places no restriction on Noe's untap step, so during Noe's untap step Noe (the active player) untaps Ahn-Crop Crasher along with their other permanents as a turn-based action [502.3], [703.4c]. This is exactly the case covered by the card ruling: if you gain control of another player's creature until end of turn and exert it, it untaps during that player's untap step [Ahn-Crop Crasher ruling #4].

Note that no player gets priority during the untap step, so nothing can be done at that moment to interfere [502.4]. If Aryana somehow still controlled Ahn-Crop Crasher when Aryana's next untap step arrived, the exert effect would apply then and keep it tapped; and if it were already untapped at that time, the effect would simply expire doing nothing [Ahn-Crop Crasher ruling #2]. The answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table — what matters is that Ahn-Crop Crasher is back under Noe's control, and Noe's own untap step untaps it.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. A player exerting a permanent only causes it to not untap during that player's next untap step, not any untap step that would untap it.

entries.question: Andres controls [Strionic Resonator] and plays [Clive's Hideaway]. They activate Strionic Resonator targeting the hideaway trigger, exiling 2 cards. On their next turn, they activate Clive's Hideaway's ability to cast the exiled card. What happens as it resolves?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling that Andres may play one or both exiled cards (optionally and without paying their mana costs) provided the legendary-creature condition is met.
entries.answer:
As Clive's Hideaway's {2}, {T} ability resolves, "the exiled card" refers to both cards exiled by the Hideaway 4 trigger and its copy, so Andres may play either one, both, or neither of them without paying their mana costs — provided he controls four or more legendary creatures at that time.

Why: Hideaway 4 on Clive's Hideaway is a triggered ability that exiles a card face down [702.75a], and it is linked to Clive's Hideaway's {2}, {T} ability that refers to "the exiled card" [607.2a]. When Strionic Resonator copies that triggered ability, the copy is also linked to the same second ability, so "the exiled card" means every card exiled by the original trigger and the copy [Strionic Resonator ruling #1]. Where such a linked ability asks about "the exiled card" and gets multiple answers, it applies to all of them [Strionic Resonator ruling #3].

Practical notes: the permission is "you may play," so playing is optional and each card is played separately as the ability resolves; playing a land this way still uses no mana but does use his land play for the turn, and a nonland card is cast without paying its mana cost. The four-or-more-legendary-creatures condition is checked as Andres actually plays a card, so if he loses legendary creatures midway he can't continue. Also, Strionic Resonator's copy doesn't grant anything an ability — it just puts a second instance of the Hideaway trigger on the stack [Strionic Resonator ruling #0], and the copy's own look-at-top-four/exile choices were made separately when the copy resolved [Strionic Resonator ruling #7].

This interaction works identically in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table; nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Assuming Andres meets the stated condition, they may cast one or both exiled cards.

entries.question: Aminah has no cards in their library and activate [Words of Wind] in their upkeep. Do they lose the game?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that Words of Wind's replacement effect still applies and replaces the draw even with an empty library, so Aminah does not attempt to draw and does not lose the game.
entries.answer:
No — Aminah doesn't lose the game, provided the {1} ability of Words of Wind is active when the draw would happen.

Why: Words of Wind's ability says "The next time you would draw a card this turn, each player returns a permanent they control to its owner's hand instead." That's a replacement effect for a card draw. An effect that replaces a card draw is applied even if no cards could be drawn because the affected player's library is empty [121.6a]. So when Aminah's draw step arrives, the draw is replaced by the returning of permanents; Aminah never actually attempts to draw from the empty library, so the state-based action that makes a player who attempted to draw from an empty library lose the game never applies [121.4], [704.5b].

Timing assumption: activating Words of Wind during the upkeep step happens before Aminah's draw step, so the shield is in place for the turn's normal draw. If instead Aminah had already been required to draw from the empty library earlier (before any Words of Wind replacement was available), that attempted draw already set up the loss and Aminah would lose the next time a player would receive priority [121.4], [704.5b] — activating Words of Wind afterward wouldn't undo it. Also note the replacement only covers "the next time" one draw; a second unreplaced draw from the empty library that turn would still cause the loss. If Aminah activated Words of Wind multiple times, they choose which instance to apply and use up on each draw [Words of Wind ruling #0].

Multiplayer: the outcome for Aminah is the same with two players or more. The difference is only in scope of the replacement — "each player returns a permanent they control to its owner's hand," so at a larger table every opponent also bounces one of their permanents.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Even though there are no there are no cards in Aminah's library and therefore no cards could be drawn, Words of Wind's replacement effect will still apply and replace the draw as normal.

entries.question: Allan controls [Living Inferno]. They activate it, targeting Nathaly's [Runeclaw Bear]. In response, Nathaly casts [Chemister's Trick], targeting the Living Inferno. How much damage will be dealt to Runeclaw Bear when the Living Inferno's ability resolves?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling that Living Inferno's damage division is locked in on activation, so Runeclaw Bear is dealt 8 damage despite Chemister's Trick.
entries.answer:
Runeclaw Bear is dealt 8 damage — the full amount Allan divided when activating Living Inferno's ability. Chemister's Trick's -2/-0 does not reduce it.

Because Living Inferno's ability divides damage among targets, the amount of damage is locked in as the ability is activated, based on Living Inferno's power at that time (8). Later changes to Living Inferno's power — including Chemister's Trick making it a 6/5 until end of turn — don't change how much damage the ability deals [Living Inferno ruling #0][Living Inferno ruling #1]. Runeclaw Bear (2/2) dies from the 8 damage.

By contrast, the damage the targeted creatures deal back to Living Inferno is not locked in; it's determined on resolution [Living Inferno ruling #1]. So Runeclaw Bear deals 2 damage (its power at resolution, per the general rule that damage equals power) to Living Inferno, which is a 6/5 at that point, so it survives with 2 damage marked.

Note also that Chemister's Trick makes Living Inferno "attack this turn if able," but Living Inferno will be tapped from paying {T}, and a tapped creature doesn't attack [Chemister's Trick ruling #0].

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.
